extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars and researchers in sociology/criminology and readers interested in policing, moral panics and the social analysis of crime
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework for explaining the 'mugging' panic and related crime phenomena, emphasising historical, structural and ideological forces (vs purely transactional/labelling accounts). Relevant to sociological research, historical analysis and policy critique of policing and crime discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze crime in terms of its social origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of crime in terms of its social origins: the contracted classes and the social conditions they live and work in are the shaping historical agencies (the 'criminal theme' becomes a 'social theme').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how industrial capitalism, class relations and social structures produce patterns of crime; use historical and social-contextual evidence rather than treating crime as an isolated, individual phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider individual responsibility versus social determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the balance between doctrines of individual responsibility (neo-classical) and positivist/sociological determinism which view actions as shaped by external forces beyond individual control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate explanations that attribute behaviour to individual choice against those that emphasise large social forces, institutions and constraints; note where legal practice preserves individual responsibility and where exemptions appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the influence of criminology and the 'science of crime' on legal thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise the emergence of criminology (borrowing from sociology, psychology and psychiatry) as a 'science of crime' that reshapes legal ideas and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how criminological theories and moral statistics enter legal discourse, policy-making and reform agendas; consider both conceptual shifts and practical channels of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the role of psychiatric and social-work professions as practical bearers of ideologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The psychiatric professions and the development of social-work agencies are the 'practical bearers' of positivist/therapeutic ideologies that modify criminal law (providing treatment-based alternatives and exemption arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how professional/para‑professional institutions translate ideas into legal exemptions, court practices (e.g., diminished responsibility, therapeutic disposals) and welfare‑oriented interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether liberal reforms operate as marginal exemptions or as transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether liberal or welfare-oriented reforms modify the core principles of criminal law or operate mainly as marginal 'exemptions' (with juvenile court as a noted exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for domains where social-work/psychiatric logic dominates (e.g., juvenile justice) versus where classical legal principles remain central; assess the institutional embedding and permanence of reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate cultural penetration and popular acceptance of reformist ideologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which liberal-reforming ideologies have reorganised popular conceptions of crime and law; the text argues liberalism largely fails to touch popular consciousness and is often seen as 'soft'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media coverage, public opinion, moral entrepreneurship and examples of 'misjudgements' (e.g., high-profile social worker errors) to judge ideological purchase and resilience under stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for class-based attitudes and internal divisions in responses to welfare reformism
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the complex, often contradictory working-class attitudes to welfare reformism (suspicion of 'state snoopers', distrust of middle-class 'do-gooders', resentment about distributional choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate working-class responses by internal segmentations (respectables/roughs, racial fractions) and link these to political alignment, material interests and party politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the 'problem of authority' and crises of hegemony
rubrics_metrics.description: Move beyond ideologies of crime to analyse the conditions and forms of the exercise of authority: a 'crisis of authority' is a crisis of hegemony or of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate when and why cross-class alliances around authority form, and analyse the institutional and ideological work required to mobilise support for authority in moments of instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogate timing: societal reaction can precede the appearance of a crime pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the hypothesis that a vigorous societal reaction to 'mugging' (or other phenomena) can appear before there are actual muggings to react to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine predispositions to panic, historical context, media framing and earlier tensions (e.g., police–community relations) to test whether reaction precedes incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate changes in offender social composition and the political meaning of crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether shifts in the social composition of offenders or infusion of political meaning into acts can trigger sudden public attention to a crime (not merely rises in raw numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypothetical and empirical checks (who is committing offences, symbolic meanings attached, e.g., political slogans or group identities) to explain why attention intensifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically evaluate the use and presentation of criminal statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether official increases in crime correspond to actual rises in incidents; challenge the validity and interpretation of criminal statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize how statistics are produced, categorised and publicised (see earlier critique referenced in Chapter 1); beware of conflation of categories (e.g., pickpocketting relabelled as 'mugging').

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh transactional/labelling explanations against historical/structural explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider transactional (labelling, micro-interaction) perspectives which show crime/control as relational, but complement them with long-term structural and historical forces shaping those transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate micro-level insights about labelling and policing interactions with macro-level analysis of legal institutions, economic conjunctures and historical forces rather than privileging one level alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the effects of intensified policing on measured crime and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that specialised policing (e.g., Anti‑Mugging Squads) can both amplify recorded crime (more detection/categorisation) and exert deterrent or displacement effects; policing can also contribute to the definition of particular offences as sites of struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how concentration of police resources, anticipatory policing, plain‑clothes operations and selective enforcement alter detection rates, offender behaviour and the social meaning of offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish crimes consonant with societal norms from crimes expressing social protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw provisional distinctions between acts that are deviant in means but broadly consonant with societal norms (ordinary crime) and acts that express elements of social protest or opposition to the existing order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify incidents by intent, context and relation to wider political/economic struggles; use this to judge whether responses should be seen as 'normalised repression' or as reactions to deeper upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess proportionality between perceived threat and scale of containment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate discrepancies between the scale of the perceived 'threat' (even as measured officially) and the scale of measures taken to contain it; disproportionate responses may signal wider historical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparisons of official estimates, public alarm, and policy responses to identify moments where 'more than normal' control correlates with periods of social or economic crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historically located, differentiated analysis rather than simplistic inversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a historically situated, differentiated analysis that links specific criminal-and-control events to the larger historical conjuncture rather than reducing phenomena to simple inversions (e.g., 'the state invented the crime').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissing the authenticity of crimes while also refusing purely functionalist or conspiracy explanations; unpack background forces and their concrete mediations in local transactions.
